title: Platform alert routing and escalation playbook
author: Lena Chen
body:
Summary:

This playbook documents the canonical alert taxonomy, routing policies, escalation procedures, dashboard templates, and retrospective checklist for platform incidents affecting core systems and services (serving-runtime, routing-gateway, control-plane, batcher, kv-cache). It codifies decisions we expect on-call engineers and incident commanders to follow and includes examples of Grafana/Prometheus queries, runbook snippets, and remediation patterns.

Scope:
- Production clusters (hosted + dedicated) and the control-plane components used by Redwood Console and Private deployments.
- Alerting, dashboarding, and triage workflows for platform teams: eng-platform, eng-serving-runtime, eng-sre, and customer-success for high-severity customer impact.

Owner & Contacts:
- Primary owner: Eng Platform (pager: #eng-platform-pager)
- Secondary support: Eng SRE (pager: #eng-sre-oncall)
- Emergency exec notify: Head of Engineering (pager: exec-oncall)
- Slack channels: #platform-ops (ops focus), #incident-command (IC communication)

Service SLOs (excerpt):
| Service | Primary SLO | Measurement window | Target | Alert trigger |
| serving-runtime | request p99 latency (token gen) | 1h rolling | <= 120ms | p99 > 180ms for 10m |
| routing-gateway | 95th percentile request latency | 1h rolling | <= 50ms | p95 > 120ms for 5m |
| control-plane | API availability | 24h rolling | >= 99.95% | error rate > 0.5% for 15m |
| kv-cache | cache hit rate | 1h rolling | >= 85% | hit-rate < 70% for 10m |

Alert taxonomy (recommended minimum):
- Sev0 (Critical): customer-facing outage, data loss, or control-plane down. Pager immediately; escalate to IC and exec.
- Sev1 (High): degraded throughput/latency causing visible customer impact > 5% of requests. Pager to platform oncall.
- Sev2 (Medium): internal degradation, degraded metrics but mitigations in place. Notify via channel.
- Sev3 (Low): informational alerts, anomalies that require engineering review. No immediate paging.

Alert routing matrix (example):
- If alert.category == "serving-latency" AND severity >= Sev1 => route to #eng-serving-runtime-oncall + #eng-platform-pager.
- If alert.category == "control-plane" AND severity == Sev0 => route to #eng-sre-oncall, exec-oncall, and customer-success-run.
- If alert involves capacity (GPU pool) => route to #gpu-fleet-team + #eng-platform-pager.

Example Prometheus/Grafana panels and queries (copyable):
- Serving runtime p99 token latency (Grafana / Prometheus):
  sum(rate(serving_request_duration_seconds_bucket{le=~".*"}[5m])) by (le) -> use histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(serving_request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])) by (le))
  Panel: p99 token gen latency (1m/5m/1h tabs)
- Error rate (control-plane):
  increase(control_plane_http_requests_total{code=~"5.."}[15m]) / increase(control_plane_http_requests_total[15m])
- Cache hit ratio (kv-cache):
  sum(kv_cache_hits_total[10m]) / (sum(kv_cache_hits_total[10m]) + sum(kv_cache_misses_total[10m]))

Alert payload standard (incoming from Alertmanager or PagerDuty):
- Fields we require in every alert: title, service, severity, current_value, threshold, graph_url, runbook_url, first_triggered, owner_team
- Example payload snippet: title: "serving-runtime p99 > 180ms"; service: "serving-runtime"; severity: Sev1; current_value: 212ms; threshold: 180ms; graph_url: <grafana-link>; runbook_url: <this-page>

Escalation & triage procedure (step-by-step):
1) Acknowledge: On-call acknowledges in PagerDuty within 2m for Sev0/Sev1.
2) Initial triage (5–10m):
   - Look at dashboard: p99, p50, error rate, request rate, cluster utilization, recent deploys.
   - Check recent alerts and logs (ELK/Datadog).
3) Classify the incident: network, infra (node), runtime (serving), control-plane, or traffic surge.
4) Mitigate: Apply a short-term mitigation using one of the approved patterns (listed below).
5) Communicate: Create an incident thread in #incident-command, set status: investigating/mitigated/resolved. Notify Customer Success for customer-impacting incidents.
6) Postmortem owner: assign a postmortem lead within 48h for Sev0/Sev1.

Approved mitigations (fast follow actions):
- Fallback routing: switch incoming traffic to fallback model variants or lower-cost region via routing-gateway: run "rwgctl route set --policy=fallthrough --target=fallback-model"
- Autoscale bump: if cluster CPU/GPU saturating, trigger reserved autoscale policy (only if safe): run "infractl autoscale bump --pool serving-gpu --minutes 30 --reason=incident"
- Disable noncritical features: turn off large-batch jobs and background analytics for 15m.
- Increase batch timeout: for throughput issues, temporarily increase batch_window_ms by 50% in serving-runtime config and reload.

Runbook snippets (common commands):
- Check node health (k8s): kubectl get nodes -o wide --selector=pool=serving-gpu\- Check pods: kubectl -n serving-system get pods -o wide | egrep "CrashLoop|OOM|Error"\- Restart a failing service (graceful): kubectl rollout restart deployment/serving-runtime -n serving-system\- Revert last deploy: ./deploy/revert.sh --service serving-runtime --rev <previous_sha>

Incident archetypes & playbooks (short):
- High p99 latency (serving-runtime):
  1. Confirm p99 across regions. If only a region: ops region isolation.
  2. Check KV cache hit-rate; if hit-rate < 60%, invalidate suspect keys and warm cache.
  3. Toggle batch window down to reduce tail latency.
  4. If latency persists and error rate rises, shift traffic to fallback variants and scale pool.
- GPU node OOM / Evictions:
  1. Identify pods causing OOM via kube events.
  2. Cord on the node: kubectl cordon <node> && drain with --ignore-daemonsets if safe.
  3. Restart runtime pods on healthy nodes.
  4. Open a bug to investigate memory growth; attach heap profiler and GPU memory dumps.
- Control-plane API errors:
  1. Check control-plane DB connection pool metrics.
  2. Scale control-plane replicas (if stateless) and check leader election.
  3. If DB is degraded, fail traffic to read-only mode and notify customers.

Dashboard & alert hygiene checklist (for engineers creating alerts/dashboards):
- Every alert must include a link to a runbook and contact owner.
- Avoid paging for noisy metrics: add hysteresis (for example, trigger only after X consecutive windows or 3/5 evaluations).
- Set distinct alert paths for capacity vs. functional errors.
- Dashboards should have a one-line summary, owner, and last reviewed date.

Template: Dashboard metadata (copyable):
Title: Serving runtime - latency and errors
Owner: eng-serving-runtime
Last reviewed: 2026-01-12
Summary: Key latency percentiles, error rates, request rates, and top 10 slowest endpoints.
Panels: p50/p95/p99 latency, request rate, error rate, CPU/GPU utilization, cache hit-rate, topology map.
How-to: Create an alert (recommended steps):
1) Design the alert metric and SLO alignment.
2) Author query and verify against historical data for at least 7 days.
3) Set an appropriate severity and routing (use this page's matrix).
4) Add runbook_url and graph_url in the alert payload.
5) Add labels: service, owner_team, severity, category.
6) Request a reviewer from eng-sre and eng-serving-runtime; schedule a short 20m review session.

Retrospective and postmortem requirements:
- For Sev0/Sev1 incidents: publish a postmortem within 7 days; include timeline, root cause(s), mitigations, follow-ups with owners and ETA.
- Follow-ups should be tracked in the incident board (Jira) and owners assigned.
- Use the blameless format and include measurable action items.

Roadmap items (near-term):
- Q2 2026: Automated routing fallback tool (rwgctl v2) that can shift traffic via policy definitions with canned rollbacks.
- Q3 2026: Alert noise reduction initiative: machine-learning deduplication + throttling before paging.
- Q4 2026: Unified dashboard for customer-impact incidents that aggregates customer session IDs and SLA exposure by account.

Notes on usage:
This document is intended to be the first-stop reference for platform on-call, incident commanders, and SREs. Teams are expected to link from service-level dashboards directly to the relevant section of this page and to keep dashboard metadata up-to-date.
